clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of the third and final step of pyrimidine degradation, caused by biallelic variants in UPB1 encoding beta-ureidopropionase (beta-alanine synthase).

The enzyme hydrolyses N-carbamyl-beta-alanine and N-carbamyl-beta-aminoisobutyrate to beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate; its deficiency causes accumulation and urinary excretion of these ureidopropionate/ureidoisobutyrate intermediates.
It is the most distal of the three inherited pyrimidine catabolism disorders, downstream of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency and dihydropyrimidinase deficiency.

The clinical spectrum is very broad and non-specific, ranging from apparently asymptomatic individuals detected on urinary screening to neurodevelopmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, movement disorder and autistic features.

Diagnosis rests on urine organic acid / amino acid analysis showing raised N-carbamyl-beta-alanine and N-carbamyl-beta-aminoisobutyric acid, often best resolved by tandem mass spectrometry, and confirmed by UPB1 molecular testing.
As with the upstream pyrimidine defects, affected individuals may have altered handling of fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy, so a personal or family history is relevant before such drugs are used.
No specific disease-modifying treatment exists; care is supportive and directed at developmental, neurological and epilepsy management.
Because many identified cases are ascertained incidentally, caution is needed before attributing a child's neurological phenotype solely to this biochemical finding.
reference.pathophysiology: Beta-ureidopropionase deficiency arises from loss-of-function variants in UPB1, which encodes beta-ureidopropionase (also called beta-alanine synthase), the enzyme catalysing the third step of the reductive pyrimidine degradation pathway. This pathway sequentially converts uracil and thymine, via dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase, into the ring-opened ureido compounds N-carbamyl-beta-alanine (from uracil) and N-carbamyl-beta-aminoisobutyrate (from thymine); beta-ureidopropionase then hydrolyses these to beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyric acid, liberating ammonia and carbon dioxide. When the enzyme is deficient, the two N-carbamyl intermediates accumulate and are excreted in urine, while production of the end-product beta-alanine, a precursor of the neuromodulatory dipeptides and a compound with inhibitory neurotransmitter-like properties, is reduced. The mechanism by which these disturbances produce neurological injury is not fully established, and the poor genotype-phenotype correlation, with the same variants seen in both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals, suggests that additional genetic or environmental modifiers determine outcome.
additionalDifferentials: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency (first-step pyrimidine degradation defect)
Dihydropyrimidinase deficiency (second-step defect, with raised dihydrouracil and dihydrothymine)

additionalInvestigations: Urinary amino acid and organic acid analysis demonstrating elevated N-carbamyl-beta-alanine and N-carbamyl-beta-aminoisobutyric acid
Tandem mass spectrometry quantification of pyrimidine degradation metabolites in urine and plasma
UPB1 gene sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis to confirm the diagnosis
Plasma and cerebrospinal fluid amino acid profiling when a central phenotype is present
Neuroimaging with MRI to characterise any structural or white-matter changes
Electroencephalography where seizures or paroxysmal events are suspected
redFlags: New or poorly controlled seizures in an affected infant
Severe or unexpected toxicity following fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy in a patient or relative
Regression or loss of acquired developmental milestones
Feeding difficulty and marked hypotonia in the neonatal period
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is highly variable and depends on the neurological phenotype rather than the biochemical defect itself: many individuals are asymptomatic with a normal outlook, whereas those with significant developmental delay, epilepsy or movement disorder have outcomes determined by the severity of these features. No treatment is known to reverse the enzymatic block.
pitfalls: Assuming causation between the biochemical abnormality and a neurodevelopmental phenotype, given that asymptomatic individuals share identical variants.
Confusing the metabolite pattern with the upstream dihydropyrimidinase or dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase defects if only limited analytes are measured.
Overlooking the relevance of the diagnosis to fluoropyrimidine drug safety in the patient and relatives.
Missing the disorder because urinary N-carbamyl amino acids are not detected on routine amino acid screens without appropriate methodology.
Attributing an isolated beta-aminoisobutyric aciduria, a common benign trait, to this enzyme deficiency.
